question.en: What is trunk-based development?

options: Merging small changes to main often
Keeping one long branch per feature
Releasing only from tagged branches
Freezing main until each release
answer: Merging small changes to main often

explanation.en: Developers integrate into one main branch at least daily, keeping branches short-lived so merges stay small.

question.en: What is a cloud spot instance?

options: A dedicated host for one tenant
Cheap capacity that can be reclaimed
A VM reserved for a year, billed up front
A burstable VM with CPU credits
answer: Cheap capacity that can be reclaimed

explanation.en: Spot capacity is sold at a deep discount because the provider can take it back at short notice.

question.en: What does this command do?

options: Exposes the pod publicly on port 8080
Tunnels local port 8080 to pod port 80
Changes the pod's container port to 8080
Creates a Service that maps 8080 to 80
answer: Tunnels local port 8080 to pod port 80

explanation.en: It opens a temporary tunnel from your machine to the pod, handy for debugging without exposing anything.

question.en: What does MTTR usually measure?

options: Average time between two failures
Time from commit to production
Average time to restore service
Share of deploys that cause incidents

explanation.en: Mean time to recovery tracks how quickly incidents are resolved; MTBF is the time between failures.

question.en: What does the restart policy do here?

options: Never restarts the container after it exits
Restarts it only when the exit code is nonzero
Restarts it once and then gives up for good
Restarts it unless you stopped it by hand
answer: Restarts it unless you stopped it by hand

explanation.en: unless-stopped restarts the container after crashes and daemon restarts, but respects a manual docker stop.

question.en: In GitOps, what normally triggers a deploy?

options: A commit to the config repo
An engineer running kubectl
A ticket approved in Jira
A nightly cron on the server
answer: A commit to the config repo

explanation.en: An agent such as Argo CD or Flux watches Git and reconciles the cluster to match whatever was merged.

question.en: What does a CrashLoopBackOff status mean?

options: The container keeps exiting
The image cannot be pulled
The node is out of memory
The pod is waiting for a free node

explanation.en: The container starts and exits repeatedly, so the kubelet waits longer before each restart.

question.en: What does a Helm chart's values.yaml hold?

options: The chart's rendered manifests
The release history of the chart
Default inputs for the templates
Credentials for the chart registry

explanation.en: Templates read from .Values; users override the defaults with -f or --set at install time.

question.en: Where does Kubernetes keep its cluster state?

options: On each node's local disk
Inside the kube-proxy cache
In the container registry
In etcd, a key-value store

explanation.en: The API server persists every object in etcd, so backing up etcd backs up the cluster.

question.en: When does an Ansible handler run?

options: After every task in the play
Only before the first task
When a task notifies it
Only if the play has failed

explanation.en: Handlers run at the end of the play, and only if a changed task notified them, e.g. to restart a service.

question.en: Why give a private subnet a NAT gateway?

options: Outbound access, no inbound
Public IPs for every host
Faster traffic between zones
DNS names for each instance

explanation.en: Instances can reach the internet for updates while nothing outside can open a connection to them.

question.en: How does an SLA differ from an SLO?

options: It is an internal target
It carries penalties if missed
It is measured per request
It is always the stricter of the two

explanation.en: An SLA is a contract with customers that has consequences; SLOs are internal targets, usually set tighter.

question.en: What is OpenTelemetry?

options: A paid hosted monitoring service
A log format used only by Kubernetes
A Prometheus alerting extension
A vendor-neutral telemetry standard

explanation.en: It provides APIs, SDKs and a collector for traces, metrics and logs that can export to any backend.

question.en: What does this workflow setting do?

options: Runs every job of the workflow in parallel
Cancels older runs for the same ref
Retries failed jobs until they pass
Limits the workflow to one runner
answer: Cancels older runs for the same ref

explanation.en: Runs sharing a concurrency group queue up; cancel-in-progress stops the stale one so only the newest commit deploys.

question.en: What role does CMD play here?

options: It replaces the ENTRYPOINT
It runs before the ENTRYPOINT
It only runs during the build
It supplies default arguments

explanation.en: With both in exec form, CMD becomes default arguments to ENTRYPOINT and is overridden by arguments to docker run.

question.en: How does a Role differ from a ClusterRole?

options: A Role can only grant read access
A Role is scoped to one namespace
A Role applies only to human users
A Role must be bound to every node
answer: A Role is scoped to one namespace

explanation.en: Roles grant permissions inside one namespace; ClusterRoles cover cluster-wide and non-namespaced resources.

question.en: Why might docker stop wait for the full timeout here?

options: The image lacks a STOPSIGNAL
The container has no HEALTHCHECK defined
A shell is PID 1 and drops SIGTERM
npm ignores every Unix signal
answer: A shell is PID 1 and drops SIGTERM

explanation.en: Shell form wraps the command in /bin/sh -c, which runs as PID 1 and does not forward SIGTERM, so Docker falls back to SIGKILL.

question.en: Which kernel feature enforces a container's memory limit?

options: Network and PID namespaces
Control groups (cgroups)
Seccomp syscall profiles
Union mount filesystems

explanation.en: Namespaces isolate what a process can see; cgroups limit and account for what it can use, such as memory and CPU.

question.en: Why prefer for_each over count for a set of buckets?

options: It creates the buckets in parallel
It skips the need for a state file
Items are keyed, so removals don't shift
It lets every bucket use a different provider
answer: Items are keyed, so removals don't shift

explanation.en: count addresses by index, so deleting one item renumbers the rest and forces replacements; for_each keys by name.

question.en: What does this change when a resource must be replaced?

options: The new one is created first
The old one is kept forever
The resource can never be destroyed
Replacement is skipped silently
answer: The new one is created first

explanation.en: Terraform normally destroys then recreates; this flips the order to avoid downtime, as long as names do not clash.

question.en: What is a startupProbe mainly for?

options: Running setup commands before the app
Delaying all traffic until the caches are warm
Choosing the node a pod boots on
Holding off liveness checks on slow boots
answer: Holding off liveness checks on slow boots

explanation.en: Liveness and readiness checks are disabled until the startup probe succeeds, so slow-starting apps are not killed mid-boot.

question.en: If no NetworkPolicy selects a pod, what traffic may reach it?

options: All traffic, in and out
Only traffic from its own namespace
Nothing until a policy allows it
Only traffic through an Ingress

explanation.en: Pods are non-isolated by default; once any policy selects a pod, only what the policies allow gets through.

question.en: Why avoid user IDs as Prometheus labels?

options: Labels cannot hold numeric values
Each value creates a new time series
Label values are limited to eight characters
Queries cannot filter on labels
answer: Each value creates a new time series

explanation.en: Every distinct label combination is its own series, so unbounded values like user IDs explode memory and query cost.

question.en: What is the main benefit of dynamic secrets, as in Vault?

options: They never need any access policy
They can be stored safely in the Git repository
One shared password for all apps
Short-lived credentials per client

explanation.en: Vault issues credentials on request with a lease, so each client gets its own and they expire or can be revoked individually.

question.en: What does depends_on guarantee here by default?

options: db is rebuilt whenever web is
db's container starts before web
web waits until db accepts connections
web restarts whenever db does

explanation.en: Plain depends_on only orders container start-up; waiting for readiness needs condition: service_healthy with a healthcheck.
